title: MTRX™ Field Guide to Screenwriting · 28 days

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: True or false: Aristotle said a good story must have three acts of equal length.
cards.answer: False. He describes a complete action with a beginning, middle and end, not Hollywood page proportions or equal acts.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: If the protagonist is interesting, can the plot be a random sequence of events?
cards.answer: Not for a tightly dramatic story. Character matters because choices make action intelligible, but the arranged action still has to alter fortune, knowledge, or both.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: In 60 words: what did Aristotle mean by putting plot before character?
cards.answer: He treated plot as the arrangement of incidents that makes fortune change, while character supplies the qualities revealed in choices. This does not make people unimportant. It means a compelling personality without consequential action is not yet dramatic. A screenplay translates inner life into choices that alter knowledge, relationships, danger or possibility.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: What are reversal and recognition?
cards.answer: Reversal turns an action toward its opposite; recognition moves a character from ignorance to knowledge. Their combination can produce a sharp emotional change.

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: Why is the Oresteia a useful case?
cards.answer: Its revenge cycle changes into a civic trial, showing that plot can transform the system in which characters act.

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: What is the safe way to use catharsis?
cards.answer: Treat it as a debated account of audience or character effect, not as a guaranteed emotional purge.

cards.name: What makes a story an action, and why does Aristotle still run Hollywood?
cards.q: Write three one-sentence ideas for your five-page short. Each must name a protagonist, an action they choose, and the cost or change that follows. Circle one whose next scene is forced by that choice.
cards.answer: A night guard hears a tiger outside an empty safari lodge and chooses to unlock the gate for a trapped child. The choice creates a visible problem, a moral cost, and a question that can drive five pages: will he protect the child, the guests, or the animal?
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: True or false: one screenplay page always equals one finished minute.
cards.answer: False. It is a useful average for normally formatted pages, but montage, silence, subtitles, dense action and editing can change the actual duration.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: Can you write that a character feels guilty in an action line?
cards.answer: Not as a private diagnosis. Write observable behaviour, sound or an object that lets the actor and audience infer guilt, unless the feeling is deliberately expressed through voice-over.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is a screenplay for?
cards.answer: A screenplay is a readable plan for a time-based audio-visual event. It gives collaborators location, time, visible action, sound and speech, while leaving room for performance, design, camera, editing and revision. It is neither a novel with shorter paragraphs nor a complete shooting plan. Its format makes a shared imagining possible.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: What are the three basic screenplay elements in the video?
cards.answer: Sluglines, action and dialogue. They locate the scene, describe observable events, and identify spoken words.

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: Why is one page per minute only a heuristic?
cards.answer: Reading density, silence, action, subtitles, montage and editing rhythm all change how long a written page becomes on screen.

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: What is the screenplay's collaborator test?
cards.answer: An actor can play it, a crew can plan it, and a reader can imagine the event without the script dictating every shot.

cards.name: What does a screenplay do that a novel cannot?
cards.q: Choose the one-sentence idea from Day 1. Draft the first half-page in master-scene form: one slugline, three short action paragraphs, and no inner diagnosis. End on a visible obstacle. Draft fast, then revise once for clarity.
cards.answer: INT. EMPTY LODGE - NIGHT A torch beam crawls across the reception desk. RAVI, 23, hears a child breathe behind the locked office door. He lifts the key. Outside, something heavy leans against the shutters. Ravi pockets the key instead. The child whispers his name.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: True or false: Aristotle invented Hollywood's three acts and page proportions.
cards.answer: False. Aristotle discusses complete action and beginning, middle and end; later screenwriting teachers supplied industrial page models.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: If a film has three acts, must Act Two be exactly half the runtime?
cards.answer: No. Percentages are drafting heuristics. A film can braid stories, delay a turn, or make the middle a series of sequences without obeying a fixed ratio.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: In 60 words: why are structure models useful if no single one is true?
cards.answer: A model gives a writer a temporary map for checking causality, escalation, information and proportion. Three acts can reveal a missing commitment; sequences can break a shapeless middle into workable units; five acts can track changing knowledge. The model earns its place only when it clarifies the story's pressure. Remove it when it flattens voice or form.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: What did Field add to the older beginning, middle and end?
cards.answer: A practical setup, confrontation and resolution paradigm with approximate page proportions and turning points.

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: What does a sequence do?
cards.answer: It gives a short stretch of action its own objective, escalation and turn while serving a larger story question.

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: What is the strongest critique of formula?
cards.answer: A mandatory template can flatten culturally or formally different stories; use models diagnostically rather than treating them as laws.

cards.name: Is there one true story structure?
cards.q: Take the idea you circled yesterday. On four cards write: ordinary world, disturbance, irreversible choice, final consequence. Rearrange the cards twice, once as three acts and once as two or three sequences. Keep the arrangement that makes the choice cause the ending.
cards.answer: Ordinary: lodge guard hides a child from a storm. Disturbance: tiger circles the shutters. Choice: he unlocks the gate. Consequence: the tiger enters, but the child is safe. The sequence wins because the spatial problem escalates without needing extra backstory.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: True or false: a logline is only marketing copy written after the screenplay.
cards.answer: False. It can market a finished script, but it is also a diagnostic. If the sentence cannot name an active protagonist, pressure and a question, the draft may not yet know its engine.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: Does high concept mean the story must be a spectacle with a huge budget?
cards.answer: No. High concept means the collision is quickly grasped and distinctive. A contained horror film can have a high-concept engine if its rule and choice are clear.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: In 60 words: what should a strong logline do?
cards.answer: A strong logline identifies a protagonist in an active situation, a goal or need, the obstacle that makes it difficult, and stakes that make the outcome matter. It also hints at the story's distinctive engine and scale. It is not a final verdict on the film. It is a portable test of whether the premise can generate scenes and choices.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: What is the difference between subject and premise?
cards.answer: A subject names an area such as grief or a haunted lodge. A premise turns that area into a situation where a character's action tests a proposition.

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: What does a producer hear in a pitch?
cards.answer: Story engine, audience promise, feasibility, scope, collaborators, risk and what makes this project distinctive now.

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: Why is high concept not synonymous with expensive?
cards.answer: A contained film can have a clear, distinctive collision or rule without large spectacle or budget.

cards.name: How do you turn an idea into a premise and a logline?
cards.q: Write three loglines for the same five-page short, each under 35 words. Version one stresses the protagonist's goal, version two the horror rule, version three the moral choice. Read them aloud and keep the one that creates the clearest dramatic question.
cards.answer: When a guilt-ridden lodge guard hears a child trapped outside during a tiger storm, he must open the gate and risk the animal entering, or leave the child to the dark. The rule, choice and stakes point toward scenes.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: True or false: a protagonist must be likeable before an audience can follow them.
cards.answer: False. Identification can mean tracking a person's perception, not approving their conduct. Curiosity, competence, vulnerability, conflict and the pleasure of watching a difficult choice can all carry attention.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: If a character has a traumatic backstory, is the character automatically deep?
cards.answer: No. A wound is material, not a personality. It becomes dramatic when it shapes a present tactic, a misreading or a choice that has a price, rather than serving as an explanatory label.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: In 60 words: how do want, need and flaw cooperate?
cards.answer: Want gives a character a playable immediate objective. A flaw is a recurring limitation in the way the character pursues it. Need names a possible change the story tests, not a guaranteed cure. Pressure makes the flaw visible, choice gives it consequence, and the audience infers the character through behaviour rather than labels.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: Why is the elevator exercise useful?
cards.answer: It holds the situation steady while changing the person's tactic. That contrast reveals priorities, fear, competence and contradiction.

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: What is the difference between liking and identification?
cards.answer: Liking asks for approval. Identification, more precisely alignment, can give access to a character's goals and perceptions without requiring allegiance.

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: When does a wound become dramatic?
cards.answer: When it shapes a present objective, tactic, misreading or costly choice. A backstory stated in dialogue is not depth by itself.

cards.name: What makes a character worth watching?
cards.q: Write it: choose the short's protagonist. Give them a concrete want, one pressure that makes the want urgent, and a choice that reveals a contradiction. Draft 8 lines freely, then underline only visible behaviour.
cards.answer: A courier wants to return a lost phone before its owner calls, but keeps refreshing the gallery. When the phone rings, he answers and lies about where he found it. The contradiction is not “he is bad”; it is that his wish to do right is fighting his hunger to see a life unlike his own.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: True or false: a scene is successful if it contains conflict.
cards.answer: False. Conflict can repeat without movement. A scene turns when the conflict changes what someone knows, can do, wants, risks or believes.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: Does “enter late, leave early” mean you should cut all context?
cards.answer: No. It means begin where the current dramatic question becomes active and leave after the decisive change. Keep context that alters interpretation, stakes or behaviour.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is a scene turn?
cards.answer: A scene turn is a meaningful change in value, knowledge, power, option, relationship or commitment. A goal meeting an obstacle is only pressure. The turn is the consequence: a refusal becomes a break, a discovery changes a plan, or a character chooses a tactic that cannot be taken back. It launches the next unit of action.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: What are the three basic scene questions?
cards.answer: What does each important character want now, what blocks it, and what changes by the exit?

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: Why is conflict alone insufficient?
cards.answer: Repeated opposition can leave the story unchanged. A turn alters information, options, power, values or relationships.

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: What does the director need from an internal feeling?
cards.answer: A playable action, visible behaviour, sound, prop or spatial choice that lets performance and staging carry the feeling.

cards.name: How does a scene turn?
cards.q: Write it: draft the first page of the short. Enter after the protagonist has already made one risky choice. Give them a goal, an obstacle, and a turn that makes the original plan harder. Draft freely, then mark the turn with a star.
cards.answer: A night guard wants to ignore a light moving inside a locked clinic. The manager calls and orders him to check it. He enters, finds a child's shoe, and hears his own name from the dark. The goal has shifted from “finish the shift” to “find who knows him.”
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: True or false: kishotenketsu means a story has no conflict or stakes.
cards.answer: False. It often avoids a direct goal versus villain engine, but a turn can create contrast, discovery, social tension, grief or a changed perspective. Stakes may be quiet and still consequential.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: Is rasa simply a list of emotions that a writer can assign to a scene?
cards.answer: No. In the Natyashastra, rasa is an aesthetic experience produced through a configuration of determinants, consequents and states, including acting, music, costume and stage convention. It is not a mood sticker.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the responsible way to borrow from another dramatic tradition?
cards.answer: Study the tradition's performance ecology, terms, history and audience assumptions before extracting a beat. Name what is being borrowed and what is not. Test the device against the short's world and intended spectator. Rasa is not a mood sticker, Noh is not slow Hollywood, and kishotenketsu is not a guarantee of conflict-free storytelling.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: What is the difference between bhava and rasa?
cards.answer: Bhava is an enacted or represented emotional state and its supporting signs. Rasa is the aesthetic flavour experienced by a prepared spectator through their configuration.

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: What does jo-ha-kyu contribute?
cards.answer: A rhythm of measured opening, development or disruption and acceleration toward conclusion, understood through Noh performance rather than as a three-act page rule.

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: Why is kishotenketsu not simply conflict free?
cards.answer: It may avoid direct goal versus villain opposition, but contrast, discovery, grief, social pressure or a changed perspective can still create movement and stakes.

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: Write it: take the same premise from Day 5 and sketch three four-line versions. Version A uses a sandhi-like progression from promise to consequence. Version B uses kishotenketsu: introduce, develop, make a surprising contrast, reconcile. Version C uses a Noh-like return of one image whose meaning changes. Choose the version that best fits your material.
cards.answer: Premise: a night guard hears a child's voice in a locked clinic. A uses escalating investigation. B shows the guard hearing the voice, finding an old recording, then recognising his own childhood room in the clinic. C repeats the corridor light three times, each return making his decision to enter less avoidable. The model borrows questions, not costumes or slogans.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: Did the rest of the world tell stories differently?
cards.q: Can you state the five-page short as a premise and a logline, then explain why its engine belongs to this form?
cards.answer: Model answer. Premise: A night guard who survives by ignoring trouble must enter a locked clinic after a child's voice calls him by name, forcing him to choose between protecting his job and confronting the memory he has buried. Logline: When a night guard hears a child calling from inside a locked clinic, he must investigate before dawn exposes him as a trespasser, but the voice leads him toward the childhood room he has spent years refusing to remember.The short uses a contained location, one urgent objective and a repeated image, so five pages can carry a complete turn. Its engine is not a monster reveal alone. The guard's want is to finish the shift safely; the pressure is the voice and the approaching manager; the contradiction is that he wants proof while fearing recognition. The final choice, entering the room, can change the value from avoidance to responsibility. A corridor light that returns three times gives the director a visual rhythm, while a kishotenketsu-like contrast can make the old recording reframe the voice without pretending to reproduce a tradition. The logline names the protagonist, goal, obstacle and stakes. It promises a filmable question: will he keep ignoring the sound, and what will recognition cost?

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: True or false: a screenplay should describe every camera angle so the director knows what to shoot.
cards.answer: False. A spec usually earns trust by describing the event, behaviour and point of view. Name a shot when the shot itself is the story, not to micromanage ordinary coverage.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: If a character is ashamed, is it acceptable simply to write SHE IS ASHAMED?
cards.answer: Usually not. Translate the diagnosis into behaviour: she hides the photograph, laughs too quickly, or turns the invitation face down. The actor and director can then discover the feeling through playable circumstances.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is visual writing?
cards.answer: Visual writing is the conversion of story pressure into observable behaviour, objects, space, sound and change. It avoids abstract diagnosis when a concrete action can carry the meaning. It also avoids decorative camera commands. The writer supplies the event and its dramatic point; the director and actors develop the precise image, movement and performance.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: Why is Plainview's silence useful?
cards.answer: It forces the screenplay and film to reveal character through effort, injury, objects, rhythm and choice rather than explanation.

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: What is the difference between a feeling label and a visual beat?
cards.answer: A feeling label names an interior state. A visual beat gives the audience behaviour or an image from which that state can be inferred.

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: When can a camera direction earn its place?
cards.answer: When the movement or point of view is itself a story event, such as a reveal, a subjective shot or a change in what the audience knows.

cards.name: How do you write what the camera sees?
cards.q: Write it: draft the first half-page of your five-page short with no dialogue. Introduce the protagonist through three actions involving the recurring object you chose in Week 1. End the half-page with a choice that makes the next scene necessary. Draft fast, then circle one image you want to protect in revision.
cards.answer: Model: “MIRA labels the empty safari jeep: RETURN BY SUNSET. She checks the fuel gauge, then quietly removes the key. A child's binoculars swing from the rear-view mirror. Mira pockets them before anyone can ask.” The object, theft and deadline show care, secrecy and pressure without naming them. The final revision question is: which action changes the story?
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: True or false: surprise and suspense are opposites, so a suspense scene must hide everything.
cards.answer: False. Suspense often gives away the danger while preserving uncertainty about timing, response, cost or outcome. Surprise hides the event; suspense makes the audience wait for it.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: If the bomb goes off after the audience has been warned, has the suspense failed?
cards.answer: No. The warning creates the pressure, but the payoff must change the situation, honour the promise and provide a new question. Hitchcock's own clip stresses relief, not a universal ban on explosions.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is Hitchcock's useful lesson about suspense?
cards.answer: Give the audience enough information to anticipate danger, then make them wait through ordinary actions, uncertain timing and a costly response. Surprise withholds the event until it arrives. Suspense exposes the possibility early but preserves uncertainty about outcome. It is not a ban on explosions; it is a design of knowledge, care and consequence.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: What is the difference between surprise and suspense?
cards.answer: Surprise is an unexpected information change. Suspense is anxious anticipation created by information, uncertainty, probability and emotional investment.

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: Why can a known threat remain frightening?
cards.answer: Because timing, response, moral choice and consequence remain uncertain, and the audience is aligned with someone who may fail.

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: What does the audience-first director ask?
cards.answer: Who knows the threat, what does the character misread, when does the audience update its model, and what choice becomes unavoidable?

cards.name: Why is suspense stronger than surprise?
cards.q: Write it: take the protagonist and recurring object from your five-page short. Draft a one-page suspense scene in which the audience knows one danger before the protagonist does. Give the protagonist a harmless task that delays recognition. End not with the threat attacking, but with a choice that reveals what the protagonist values. Then draft a second version in which the protagonist sees the threat first.
cards.answer: Model: “The phone vibrates inside the locked birdhouse. NILA keeps watering the garden. The screen lights through the slats: HOME. She turns the tap off. A second vibration. She lifts the birdhouse, hears breathing, and sets it back.” The dread comes from delay and care, not a loud entrance. The revision test is whether the choice to set it back tells us who Nila is.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: True or false: good film dialogue should sound exactly like real life.
cards.answer: False. Screen dialogue is compressed and selective. It can be realistic, heightened, comic or stylised, but it must feel true to this character in this pressure.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: If a scene contains important information, should the characters explain it to each other so the audience cannot miss it?
cards.answer: Usually no. Let information arrive through a goal, an obstacle or a tactic. Characters who already know a fact rarely recite it unless they are using the reminder to accuse, persuade or conceal.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: In 60 words: why is realistic dialogue not enough?
cards.answer: Real speech is often repetitive, unfocused and private. Screen dialogue compresses it into a character-specific action. A line should reveal voice, pursue a want, create or resist pressure, deliver necessary information, or alter the relationship. Natural surface helps, but dramatic truth comes from the character's tactic and the scene's changing power.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: What makes a voice distinct?
cards.answer: Repeatable choices in vocabulary, syntax, rhythm, what the character notices and what the character refuses to name.

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: How should exposition enter a conversation?
cards.answer: Through a present goal or conflict that gives the speaker a reason to reveal, distort, withhold or weaponise the information.

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: What is a playable action?
cards.answer: An immediate verb an actor can pursue, such as persuade, threaten, reassure, stall, recruit or punish.

cards.name: How do you write dialogue that does not sound written?
cards.q: Write it: take the central scene of your five-page short and write a one-page dialogue version between the protagonist and the person who blocks the want. Give each person a different public goal and private fear. Draft without polishing. On revision, underline every line that only explains backstory, then replace at least two with tactics, objects, interruptions or a change of subject.
cards.answer: Model: “RAVI: You said the gate was locked. LEENA keeps counting the keys. LEENA: I said it was closed. RAVI: That is not the same word. LEENA: You always liked the precise word.” The argument appears to be about language, but the keys and correction expose blame. Each line pushes, evades or tests.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: True or false: the writer must decide a theme sentence before writing the first page.
cards.answer: False. A theme can guide a draft, but it often becomes clear through repeated choices, contradictions and revision. Discover first, then name the pattern.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: If a film has a political idea, must its characters speak the thesis aloud?
cards.answer: No. Let institutions, spaces, rules and consequences embody the idea. A character can state a belief, but the plot should test it rather than simply reward the speech.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: In 60 words: how does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.answer: Theme emerges when a story repeats a question through images, rules and choices, then makes characters pay different costs for their answers. A controlling idea can guide revision, but the audience should encounter evidence and contradiction rather than a lecture. Motifs help the pattern gather emotional force. The ending should complete a choice, not merely announce a moral.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: What is the difference between theme and message?
cards.answer: Theme is an explored question or pattern of value and consequence. A message is a more direct proposition the audience is asked to accept.

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: How does Pan's Labyrinth dramatise authority?
cards.answer: Vidal, Carmen, the faun, Mercedes and Ofelia repeat the pressure of commands and refusals across the historical and fantasy worlds.

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: What makes a motif thematic?
cards.answer: It recurs with changed meaning or consequence, so the audience connects the image to the story's central pressure.

cards.name: How does theme emerge without preaching?
cards.q: Write it: make a three-row theme ladder for your five-page short. Choose one question. In row one, show the protagonist performing the safe or habitual answer. In row two, force the same question through a new object or relationship. In row three, make the climax a costly physical choice that answers without naming the theme. Draft the rows as scenes, not explanations.
cards.answer: Model: question, “When does protection become control?” Row one: AMAL hides the spare key from her brother. Row two: she locks his phone during a storm and calls it help. Row three: she must hand him the key to let him rescue a neighbour. The theme emerges from the changing meaning of the same protective act.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: True or false: every line of dialogue should have a hidden meaning.
cards.answer: False. Direct speech can be the right style, especially for blunt comedy, ritual, or a deliberate absence of mystery. Subtext is a tool, not a fog machine.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: If a character says “I am fine” while hiding an injury, is the subtext simply “I am not fine”?
cards.answer: Not necessarily. The playable action might be protect my friend, preserve status, avoid pity, or force you to ask again. Name the tactic, not only the concealed fact.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is subtext?
cards.answer: Subtext is the meaning produced when a spoken line or visible action meets a specific context, history, power relation and immediate tactic. It is not a code with one answer. Write the circumstance and the playable pursuit, then let performance, blocking and editing reveal what the character avoids saying or cannot yet understand.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: What are text and context?
cards.answer: Text is the spoken line or observable action. Context is the surrounding situation, history, stakes and power that alter how the audience reads it.

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: What makes an intention playable?
cards.answer: It names an action a character can pursue, such as persuade, conceal, recruit or make him stay, rather than an abstract state such as sadness.

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: How can an object carry subtext?
cards.answer: Give it a repeated or chosen action whose meaning changes with the relationship, such as smoothing a receipt, withholding a cup, or returning a key.

cards.name: What is subtext, and how can an actor play it?
cards.q: Write it: take your short film's central scene. Give the protagonist a public goal and a private goal. Draft six lines of direct dialogue first, then revise so three lines pursue the public goal while an action, interruption or silence exposes the private one. Keep the scene playable and let the turn change who has power.
cards.answer: Model: “You can keep the spare key,” Mira says. She places it beside the kettle, not in his hand. “I only need it for the plants.” He pockets the key. “They'll be fine.” She turns the kettle on though it is already hot. The public action is logistics. The private action is an attempt to make departure reversible. The key becomes the turn: he accepts access without promising return.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: True or false: a horror film must show a monster early to keep its promise.
cards.answer: False. The promise may be unease, violation, pursuit, transformation or the fear that a safe social space is unsafe. A withheld monster can intensify the contract if the surrounding evidence keeps accumulating.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: If the audience can predict the genre, is the story unoriginal?
cards.answer: No. Familiar expectation is the surface on which invention can work. The writer can make the fear specific to a character, change the moral meaning of the convention, or turn a comic rhythm into a threat.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is a genre contract?
cards.answer: A genre contract is the emotional and narrative expectation a work establishes with its audience. Horror may promise danger in a safe space, comedy may promise tension released through incongruity, and a hybrid may move between them. The writer can satisfy, complicate or invert conventions, but the break should remain specific to the film's world and character.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: What does Peele mean by pattern and break?
cards.answer: Repeated expectation builds tension or anticipation. A meaningful break releases that pressure as laughter, fear, surprise or another visceral response.

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: How does Get Out turn politeness into horror?
cards.answer: It repeats ordinary social rituals, then makes their explanations less safe. The audience rereads hospitality as a system of control around Chris.

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: What is the difference between an inversion and a random twist?
cards.answer: An inversion changes a recognised convention while remaining grounded in the story's promise. A random twist surprises without being prepared by the film's pattern or stakes.

cards.name: What does a genre promise, and how does horror keep it?
cards.q: Write it: choose the genre contract for your 5-page short in one sentence. On five lines, mark the promise, the first pattern, the escalation, the break, and the new rule after the break. Then write one image that makes the genre legible before any explanation.
cards.answer: Model: Contract: “A quiet eco-thriller makes a routine wildlife call feel unsafe.” Pattern: the ranger hears one bird call at each checkpoint. Escalation: the call moves closer despite the empty map. Break: the caller answers from inside her locked jeep. New rule: the forest is repeating her route, not guiding it. The horror grows from sound and geography, not a pasted monster.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: True or false: a good outline must predict every line before drafting.
cards.answer: False. It needs enough pressure and direction to make the next writing decision visible. If the outline kills a better discovery, change the outline.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: If you draft freely, should you avoid all planning?
cards.answer: No. Planning can happen before, during or after pages. A discovery writer can outline the next sequence after seeing what the previous scene reveals.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: In 60 words: how does outlining help a discovery writer?
cards.answer: Outlining externalises the story after or during discovery. It groups scenes into movements, exposes repeated beats, tests cause and effect, and shows where a short needs a choice rather than more explanation. Because the map is provisional, the writer can change it when a freewritten scene reveals a stronger character action or ending.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: Why did Gulino revive the sequence idea?
cards.answer: To make the feature middle manageable by treating it as smaller scripts that each build toward a new problem.

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: What belongs on a scene card?
cards.answer: A concrete event, the character's immediate pursuit, the obstacle or pressure, and the changed question or consequence at the end.

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: What is the difference between a map and a contract?
cards.answer: A map guides choices and can change when discovery improves the story. A contract treats the plan as fixed, even when the draft reveals a better route.

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: Write it: make the one-page outline for your own five-page short. Use three sections: baseline and disturbance, the attempt that creates a cost, and the decisive choice plus final image. Under each section list two or three scene cards. Write freely for five minutes, then circle the one card where the protagonist cannot return to the old situation.
cards.answer: Model: Baseline: Nila records frog calls at a dry lake. Disturbance: her recorder captures a call from a species declared extinct. Attempt: she follows it at night and finds the sound coming from her own abandoned field notebook. Cost: the notebook contains tomorrow's recording, in her handwriting. Choice: she burns the notebook, then hears the call from the dark. Final image: the recorder light blinks while Nila walks away without taking it. The outline keeps discovery in the image while the causal spine stays clear.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do you outline without killing discovery?
cards.q: Boss fight: produce a character sheet and a one-page outline for your five-page short. Include the protagonist's want, fear, contradiction, public goal, private need, antagonist or opposing force, genre contract, central dramatic question, three sequences, and final image. What would a strong answer look like?
cards.answer: Model project: The Last Call.Character sheet: Nila, 24, a field-recordist who maps frogs around a drying lake. Want: prove that the lake still contains a rare frog before the survey closes. Fear: that attention makes her complicit in the place's destruction. Contradiction: she wants evidence to save the lake, but treats every living thing as data. Public goal: find and record the call. Private need: choose care over possession. Opposing force: the deadline, the dry landscape and the part of Nila that will not stop recording. Genre contract: a quiet ecological horror in which a familiar sound makes a safe route impossible. Dramatic question: will Nila keep the recording if it proves the lake is listening back?One-page outline: 1. Baseline and disturbance. At dusk, Nila labels empty sample bags beside the dry lake. Her recorder captures a frog call that should not exist. She checks the waveform, then hears the same call from behind her. She turns, but the shore is empty. 2. Attempt and cost. Nila follows the call through reeds and places the recorder beneath a broken sign. The call repeats from the recorder before she presses record. Inside her field notebook she finds tomorrow's time stamp in her own handwriting. She tears out the page. The lake answers from the direction of her car, forcing her to choose between leaving and taking the evidence. 3. Choice and image. Nila returns to the recorder, removes its battery, and walks toward the road. The call continues from the dead machine. She leaves it behind. In the final image, the empty recorder light blinks once as the lake goes silent.The outline works because each attempt changes the available choice, the horror grows from the project's ordinary tool, and the final image proves Nila has surrendered ownership of the evidence. Your version can be quiet, comic, romantic or brutal. Keep the causal spine, then let your own strange image replace mine.

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: True or false: Campbell published the twelve-step screenplay template used in development rooms.
cards.answer: False. Campbell published a comparative myth theory. The familiar twelve-stage writing tool came later through Christopher Vogler.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: If a story has no quest, does it have no structure?
cards.answer: No. A story can organise change through recognition, relationship, community, ritual, investigation or a changed perception of place.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the difference between Campbell and Vogler?
cards.answer: Campbell proposed a comparative myth pattern organised around departure, initiation and return, and argued for its recurrence across cultures. Vogler transformed that scholarship into a seven-page Disney development memo, adding film-friendly stages, archetypes and examples. Campbell is a theory of myth. Vogler is a practical screenwriting lens. Neither is a universal law.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: What were Campbell's three broad movements?
cards.answer: Departure, Initiation and Return, expanded through episodes such as call, threshold, trials, ordeal, reward and return.

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: What did Vogler's memo add?
cards.answer: A concise, film-facing twelve-stage vocabulary and examples designed for story analysis and development conversations.

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: What is the ethical craft test?
cards.answer: Ask whether the model clarifies this character and culture. If it erases specific values or forces a return that the story does not need, refuse it.

cards.name: Is the Hero's Journey real, or just a useful lens?
cards.q: Write it: draft the next scene of your five-page short in which the protagonist crosses a threshold, but do not call it a Hero's Journey. Show the threshold through an object, action or change of space.
cards.answer: The lift stops between floors. Mira could press the alarm, but instead she hands her phone through the gap to the stranger outside. The choice makes her enter a social world she has avoided, without a speech announcing transformation.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: Does one screenplay page always equal exactly one minute of finished film?
cards.answer: No. It is a rough estimate. Montage, silence, songs, subtitles and unusual action can make the page run shorter or longer.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: Should every line contain camera directions?
cards.answer: No. A spec script normally prioritises story action and sound. Specific visual direction belongs when the image is essential, not to prove that the writer owns a camera.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes screenplay format professional?
cards.answer: Professional format makes a time-based audio-visual plan quickly legible to readers and collaborators. Sluglines locate scenes, action lines describe visible behaviour and sound, character cues organise dialogue, and selective parentheticals prevent confusion. Conventions support breakdowns and revision, but they do not create drama. Clear choices and playable action matter more than ornamental rule-following.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: What does a slugline do?
cards.answer: It identifies interior or exterior, location and approximate time, giving the scene a production coordinate.

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: What is action-line discipline?
cards.answer: Describe present-tense behaviour and sound a viewer could receive, rather than novelistic diagnosis or unfilmable backstory.

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: When does the page-a-minute rule fail?
cards.answer: When silence, montage, songs, subtitles, dense action or unusual layout changes the relationship between page space and screen time.

cards.name: What does professional screenplay format communicate?
cards.q: Write it: convert the next beat of your five-page short into a screenplay page. Use one slugline, three short action paragraphs, one character cue and no camera directions. Let an object reveal the change.
cards.answer: INT. STAIRWELL - NIGHT A phone glows on the landing. RAVI reaches for it, then hears his own voicemail playing from below. He pockets the phone without answering. The action is spare, but the sound and the withheld choice make the scene filmable.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: If a film can be labelled with all fifteen Save the Cat beats, does that prove the method caused the film to work?
cards.answer: No. A later analyst can map many stories onto a flexible list. The method is a drafting and discussion tool, not proof of causation.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: Must the protagonist get what they want before they can change?
cards.answer: No. A protagonist can lose, recognise, refuse, or change the meaning of the goal. The important question is what the final choice costs.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: In 60 words: why are structure models heuristics?
cards.answer: A structure model describes recurring movements that may help a writer plan, diagnose or discuss a story. It does not cause an audience response, guarantee originality or fit every culture and genre. Use it after identifying a premise and character pressure. Keep the model only when it sharpens an actual scene, choice, reversal or cost.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: What does Save the Cat provide?
cards.answer: Fifteen named beats and a shared development vocabulary, useful for diagnosing promise and pacing but not a mandatory studio formula.

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: What is the central causal move in Harmon's circle?
cards.answer: A character gets or reaches something they wanted, pays a price, returns and demonstrates change.

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: What does Truby add?
cards.answer: A stronger emphasis on moral weakness, opponent, desire, plan, battle, self-revelation and the story's moral argument.

cards.name: Are Save the Cat, Harmon and Truby formulas or tools?
cards.q: Write it: choose one structure lens and map only the next two pages of your five-page short. Then draft the scene without naming the beats. End on a choice that creates a cost, not on an explanation of the theme.
cards.answer: The Save the Cat label might call the moment a Catalyst. The page shows a cleaner image: after deleting the client's files, Leena sees the same files reappear on her own laptop. She can report it or hide it, and either choice makes page three harder.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: Does a first draft need to be good enough for someone else to read?
cards.answer: No. Its first job is to exist so the writer can see the whole problem and revise with evidence.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: Is writer's block proof that you have no talent?
cards.answer: No. A block can signal fear, unclear stakes, an impossible standard, a missing decision or exhaustion. Diagnose the task, not the person.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the job of a first draft?
cards.answer: A first draft discovers and records the complete dramatic route: scenes, choices, reversals, gaps and an ending. It is not the place to prove talent or polish every line. Drafting lowers the standard temporarily so the writer can see the whole object. Revision then tests structure, character, clarity, rhythm and the value of the strange details.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: What does Kaufman mean by no template?
cards.answer: A screenplay is an exploration whose form should arise from the material, not a promise that no craft choices or revision are needed.

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: What is a useful response to block?
cards.answer: Name the concrete obstacle, lower the task, write a temporary bad version and leave a marker for revision rather than judging your identity.

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: What makes a first draft professional?
cards.answer: It is complete enough to reveal the whole problem and specific enough that the next pass can make intentional choices.

cards.name: How do working writers get a first draft done?
cards.q: Write it: draft the next 60 to 90 seconds of your five-page short without editing. Give the protagonist one action they can complete, one thing they cannot say, and one visual detail that only this story would contain. Mark any gap with NEEDS RESEARCH and keep moving.
cards.answer: Nikhil records the voice note three times. On the fourth, he sends only the room tone. His mother replies with a photograph of the empty chair. The draft works because the unsent explanation becomes an action, and the image gives the next scene a question.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: True or false: a believable world needs a large quantity of factual backstory.
cards.answer: False. It needs selective facts that alter what people do. One stair, smell, uniform, timetable, or locked door can carry more dramatic weight than a page of explanation.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: If a script names a real city, does that automatically make its world specific?
cards.answer: No. A place name is a label. Specificity arrives through the local routes, prices, sounds, work, weather, etiquette, and unequal access that force characters to behave differently.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: In 60 words: how does research become dramatic world?
cards.answer: Research becomes dramatic world when a selective fact changes access, behaviour, knowledge, or cost. Translate the fact into a route, object, sound, rule, job, or threshold that characters must negotiate. Then make a choice depend on it. If the detail can be removed without changing the scene, it is probably background research, not yet story.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: What is spatial grammar?
cards.answer: The way locations, levels, thresholds, and routes express relationships and distribute power.

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: What is the research to drama test?
cards.answer: Remove the detail. If access, behaviour, knowledge, or cost stays the same, the detail has not become dramatic yet.

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: Why can genre shifts feel earned in Parasite?
cards.answer: The same material spaces and objects retain consequences while the audience's interpretation and emotional pressure change.

cards.name: How do you build a world that feels true?
cards.q: Write it: draft or revise page 3 of your five-page short. Choose one location detail that embodies the protagonist's social or material pressure. Start the scene late, make the detail block a goal, and end with the protagonist choosing a more expensive route. Do not explain the world in dialogue. Draft freely for four minutes, then underline the one image that must survive.
cards.answer: A courier reaches a clinic's locked staff entrance with a cooler of vaccines. The public door is open, but a wedding party blocks the lobby. She sees the temperature display climb one degree. She leaves the cooler with the guard and walks through the rain to the loading ramp. The detail works because the building, the heat, and the route force a choice without a speech.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: True or false: a pilot only needs a strong cliffhanger.
cards.answer: False. A cliffhanger can create a question, but the pilot must also establish a world, a point of view, characters we can follow, and a repeatable source of story.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: Does a writers' room mean that every writer writes every scene together?
cards.answer: No. The room develops story and solves problems collectively, while individual writers may be assigned episodes or drafts under the showrunner's process.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes a pilot different from a short film?
cards.answer: A pilot must satisfy an episode-sized dramatic question while establishing a world, characters, tone, and repeatable series engine. A short film can close its world more completely. Both need a present-tense objective and a turn, but the pilot also proves that future episodes can produce new choices without repeating the same scene.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: What is a series engine?
cards.answer: A repeatable source of goals, conflict, and change that can generate future episodes.

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: What is the pilot paradox?
cards.answer: The pilot must resolve an immediate dramatic problem while opening a changed system that makes return meaningful.

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: What does a room externalise?
cards.answer: Shared story decisions, continuity, character promises, production limits, and future possibilities that one writer might otherwise hold privately.

cards.name: How does television writing work?
cards.q: Write it: draft page 4 of your five-page short. Give the protagonist a repeatable routine, then break it once. In six lines of action, show the old routine, the disturbance, and the new rule. Add one line of dialogue that could begin a series but must instead make the short's final choice harder. End on a specific consequence, not a generic cliffhanger.
cards.answer: Every night, Mira photographs the locked shop shutter for insurance. Tonight the shutter is already open. Her brother says, “You can still call it an accident.” Mira deletes the photo, steps inside, and hears the camera click from the dark. The routine establishes a world rule, the break creates a choice, and the sound opens consequence without promising a television series.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: True or false: a professional screenplay must contain no visual direction at all.
cards.answer: False. Avoid vanity shot lists, but write essential point of view, reveals, sound, spatial logic, and images the story depends on. The page should communicate an experience while leaving useful choices for the director.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: If the actor is sad, is writing “she feels devastated” enough for a director?
cards.answer: No. Give circumstance and playable behaviour: she keeps smiling while folding the invitation into smaller and smaller squares. The actor can pursue an action, and the director can stage an image.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: In 60 words: how should a future director write the page?
cards.answer: Write the essential event, point of view, playable behaviour, sound, and spatial relationship that the film needs. Do not prescribe coverage merely to display taste. After the beat is clear, imagine the cut: what does the audience know before it, and what do they know after it? The page should invite a strong staging choice, not eliminate every choice.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: What is a director's breakdown?
cards.answer: A pass that identifies scene beats, point of view, objectives, obstacles, space, sound, and visual priorities.

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: What does the Kuleshov effect teach a writer?
cards.answer: Meaning can arise from the relation between adjoining images, so a cut can change how an otherwise unchanged face or object is read.

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: What is the test for camera language?
cards.answer: Keep it when the visual instruction is essential to point of view, reveal, sound, rhythm, or a meaningful absence of coverage; remove vanity directions.

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: Write it: finish page 5 of your first draft. Give the protagonist one final visible choice, then write the last image as a cut-worthy contrast with the opening image. On a second pass, annotate every scene with objective, obstacle, turn, point of view, essential prop, and sound. Replace one abstract emotion with behaviour. Do not polish dialogue yet. The milestone is a complete, imperfect first draft.
cards.answer: Opening: A clean glass sits beneath a dripping tap. Ending: the same glass is full, but Arun holds it under the locked door instead of drinking. The final image turns a repeated object into a choice. A director can stage the hand, the threshold, the sound of the drip, and the cut without being told which lens to use.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How does a director read your script?
cards.q: Can you deliver a complete first draft of your five-page short and explain the director's eye behind its last image?
cards.answer: Model answer: Yes. My first draft is a contained story about Arun, who keeps a glass beneath a leaking tap while waiting for his brother to return. The routine breaks when the brother locks himself in the next room. Arun wants entry, but needs to stop treating silence as permission to wait. The world is a rented flat with a failing tap and one locked threshold. The visual rule is repetition: each return to the glass changes its meaning. The final image must show a visible choice, not explain the theme.INT. KITCHEN - NIGHT A GLASS sits beneath a dripping tap. DRIP. ARUN, 23, checks his phone. No signal. He wipes the glass dry with his shirt. From the corridor: BROTHER (O.S.) Leave it. Arun looks at the closed bedroom door. ARUN You said ten minutes. No answer. The tap fills the silence. He moves the glass closer to the door, then stops. A thin line of water slips under it. Arun kneels. The water is warm. He presses his ear to the wood. ARUN Open up. The lock turns. Not open. Just turns. Arun steps back. The glass trembles beneath the tap. He takes it in both hands and carries it to the bedroom door. The dripping stops. Arun pours the water under the door. CUT TO BLACK.This is a rough model, not a template to copy. It establishes a filmable routine, introduces an obstacle, escalates through sound and space, and lets the final action answer the opening image. The first draft can contain awkward lines or a placeholder. Its job is to make the whole chain visible so the next pass can improve structure, performance, and images.

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: True or false: if a scene worked on the page, it must stay in the cut.
cards.answer: False. A scene earns its place by what the finished film makes the audience feel, understand or anticipate. A page can be elegant and still repeat information, slow a turn or steal agency from a later scene.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: Does a note that says cut this scene tell you exactly what to write?
cards.answer: No. It reports a possible symptom or taste. Ask what the reader felt, where they lost the thread and what they expected next, then diagnose before changing the scene.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: In 60 words: why is editing a rewrite?
cards.answer: The cut changes order, duration, point of view, sound and performance emphasis. Those changes alter what the audience knows, feels and expects, so they alter story, not merely surface. A rewrite performs the same diagnosis earlier in language. Test the largest promises first, then character agency, scene turns and finally lines.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: What should the first rewrite pass test?
cards.answer: The story promise, sequence order and ending. If the film does not create the intended question, polishing dialogue cannot rescue it.

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: What is the difference between a note and a fix?
cards.answer: A note reports an effect, confusion or desire. A fix is one possible intervention. Diagnose the repeated effect before accepting the proposed intervention.

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: What does the director watch for in a cut?
cards.answer: Playable behaviour, geography, sound, rhythm, point of view and how each juxtaposition changes audience attention.

cards.name: Why is editing the final rewrite?
cards.q: Write it: make a four-pass rewrite map for your five-page short. Spend one minute naming the story promise and ending, one on the protagonist's choice, one on each scene's goal and turn, and two on cutting one repeated line or replacing it with behaviour. Draft freely first, then mark changes in a new version.
cards.answer: Original model: “Pass 1: The boy must choose whether to open the locked clinic door. Pass 2: He wants his father's approval, but the choice proves he can act without it. Pass 3: In the corridor, remove the speech and let him pocket the key, hear the oxygen alarm, then turn back. Pass 4: Cut ‘I am not afraid’ and keep the hand shaking.” The passes move from promise to playable image.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: True or false: Chekhov said every object introduced must later be used literally.
cards.answer: False. His 1 November 1889 letter to Aleksandr Lazarev criticised a loaded rifle placed on stage when nobody intended to fire it. The point is to remove or use a conspicuous promise, not to make every background detail a weapon.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: If the audience guesses the ending, has the ending failed?
cards.answer: No. A prepared ending can be pleasurable because the audience recognises the pattern and watches the character approach its cost. Surprise is one effect; inevitability, emotional consequence and recontextualisation matter too.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes an ending surprising and inevitable?
cards.answer: Inevitability comes from evidence, causality and character choice already planted. Surprise comes from a new relation among those elements, not from information imported at the last second. A strong ending pays off the audience's active question, changes the meaning of earlier details and imposes a cost the protagonist cannot evade.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: What did Chekhov actually write in the 1889 letter?
cards.answer: He warned against putting a loaded rifle on stage if nobody intends to fire it, and against making promises. The wall-pistol wording is a later recollection.

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: What is the difference between mystery and closure?
cards.answer: Mystery organises missing knowledge and investigation. Closure resolves some central question; it can leave a character or theme open.

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: How can a director make a payoff visual?
cards.answer: Return an object, framing, sound or eyeline with changed context, then let the character's behaviour reveal the cost.

cards.name: How do great endings pay off?
cards.q: Write it: perform an ending pass on your five-page short. Circle one detail from page one or two that can return in the final page. Rewrite the last three beats so the detail affects a choice, not merely a twist. Then remove one explanatory sentence and replace it with an image or action.
cards.answer: Original model: “The boy has carried the clinic key all day but refuses the door. At the end the alarm stops. He could leave. Instead he unlocks the door, places the key on the nurse's desk, and waits.” The key pays off literally, but the waiting pays off the character's new responsibility.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: True or false: being on The Black List means a script won an official contest.
cards.answer: False. The annual list began as a survey of Hollywood executives' favourite unproduced scripts. The platform also offers paid hosting and feedback, but those are not the same thing as the annual survey.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: Can you apply to the current BBC Writers Open Call from Ahmedabad?
cards.answer: No, not under the 2026 to 2027 terms. The applicant must be resident in the UK, Channel Islands, Isle of Man or Republic of Ireland with a right to work in the UK. That is a current eligibility rule, not a judgement on the script.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: In 60 words: how are Nicholl, the Black List and BBC Writers different?
cards.answer: Nicholl is an Academy competition for feature screenplays with published judging stages and fellowships. The annual Black List is a survey of executives' most liked unproduced scripts, separate from the company's paid platform. BBC Writers is a development opportunity with current residency, length, format and submission rules. Check each year's terms.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: What is a spec?
cards.answer: A screenplay written without a prior commission, usually to demonstrate voice or attract a sale, assignment or relationship.

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: What did the Academy report for Nicholl in 2023?
cards.answer: 5,599 entries, at least two reads per script, about 5 percent to quarterfinals, about 2 percent to semifinals and about 10 to 15 finalists.

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: What is the current BBC eligibility limit you must notice?
cards.answer: The 2026 to 2027 Open Call requires UK, Channel Islands, Isle of Man or Republic of Ireland residence with a right to work in the UK; Ahmedabad residence is outside that rule.

cards.name: How does a script get read, bought and made?
cards.q: Write it: create a one-page package for your rewritten five-page short. Include a logline, one sentence on the visual promise, the number of locations and speaking roles, the rights status of any source material, a realistic production constraint, and the next ask: table read, producer note or a micro-budget shoot. Do not claim attachments you do not have.
cards.answer: Original model: “A night guard finds a child's lost shoe outside a locked clinic and must choose between protecting his job and opening the door during a power cut. One clinic corridor, two actors, one practical alarm and a five-minute running time. Original story, no underlying rights. Ask: a table read with one actor and a producer who can test the location.” It makes the film legible without overselling it.

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: True or false: write “she feels guilty” and the actor will know what to do.
cards.answer: False. Guilt is an interpretation. Give the actor a situation and a playable tactic, such as make him forgive her without admitting why she needs forgiveness.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: Does Stanislavski's system mean actors should simply remember painful experiences?
cards.answer: No. Later American Method practices often emphasised affective memory, but Stanislavski's system was broader: objectives, actions, given circumstances, physical behaviour, concentration and a coherent score of tasks. Do not reduce it to emotional autobiography.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes a scene actor-friendly?
cards.answer: An actor-friendly scene gives a specific objective, obstacles, given circumstances, a changing relationship and tactics that can be played. It does not dictate an emotion or bury the turn in explanation. The writer creates pressure and a choice; the actor discovers behaviour. The director then stages, listens and protects the scene's changing action.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: What is an objective?
cards.answer: The immediate thing a character is trying to obtain in the scene, such as make him stay, hide the key or win permission.

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: Why is an action verb better than an emotion label?
cards.answer: A verb gives the actor a tactic to pursue. “Persuade” or “test” can change in response to resistance; “feel guilty” cannot be played as a clear task.

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: What did the Group Theatre add?
cards.answer: An ensemble model, common training and new American plays, adapting Stanislavski's influence to Depression-era American theatre.

cards.name: How do you write scenes actors want to play?
cards.q: Write it: rewrite the central scene of your five-page short for actors. Put the protagonist's objective and obstacle in the margin, then replace every interior label with a visible tactic, object or interruption. Add one moment when the tactic changes. Read only the action aloud and ask whether the relationship still turns.
cards.answer: Original model: “Maya needs her brother to sign. She starts by flattering him, switches to correcting the date, then hides the pen when he asks why she is rushing. He signs with a different pen and keeps the form.” The shame is not announced. It appears as tactics that fail and a choice that changes who controls the document.
cards.label: Write it · 5 min · your short

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: True or false: the 2023 WGA MBA lets a company require a writer to use ChatGPT.
cards.answer: False. On an MBA covered project, a writer may choose to use AI if the company consents and applicable policy is followed, but the company cannot require AI use.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: If a human writes a detailed prompt, does that automatically make the resulting screenplay copyrightable?
cards.answer: No. The US Copyright Office said on March 16, 2023 and January 29, 2025 that a prompt alone normally does not determine the expressive elements sufficiently. The answer is case by case.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: In 60 words: what do the 2023 WGA MBA and US copyright guidance actually say about AI?
cards.answer: The 2023 WGA MBA governs covered employment: AI is not a writer, companies cannot force its use, and supplied AI material must be disclosed. The US Copyright Office’s March 2023 guidance and January 2025 report apply human authorship case by case: prompts alone do not suffice, while human expression, arrangement or modification may be protected. Neither settles global law.

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: Can an MBA covered company require a writer to use AI?
cards.answer: No. A writer may use it only with company consent and policy compliance; the company cannot require it.

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: What did the Copyright Office say about prompts?
cards.answer: A prompt alone normally does not determine the expressive elements enough for copyright; the inquiry is case by case.

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: What should you preserve if he uses an allowed tool?
cards.answer: A human authored draft history, the prompts and outputs where relevant, source checks, permission records and any required disclosure.

cards.name: Will AI write films, or only imitate a writer?
cards.q: Write it: take the short’s weakest scene and ask an AI system, or a friend acting as one, for three possible problems only. Do not accept generated lines. Rebuild the scene yourself, keeping a note of the human choice that fixes each problem.
cards.answer: Model: “The scene feels static because Mira only answers questions.” your rewrite gives Mira a playable action: she hides the broken recorder while answering. The tool, if used, diagnosed a possibility; the writer chose the image, action and consequence.

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: True or false: empathy means the audience must approve of the protagonist.
cards.answer: False. A viewer can understand a character’s fear or logic without endorsing the character’s choice. Identification is temporary alignment, not moral agreement.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: If a mystery hides every fact, will curiosity automatically rise?
cards.answer: No. A useful gap has a foothold. Give the audience a question, a concrete stake and enough information to form a live prediction; total confusion feels like exclusion.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: In 60 words: why can tragedy grip an audience?
cards.answer: Tragedy gives the audience a safe but emotionally serious frame for pity, fear, curiosity and recognition. Transportation absorbs attention; a shaped information gap invites prediction; identification lets viewers understand a person without approving every act. A payoff then changes knowledge or feeling. These are useful mechanisms, not laws, and catharsis remains contested.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: What is narrative transportation?
cards.answer: Absorption into a story through attention, imagery and emotion, measured as a psychological process rather than mere admiration.

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: What makes an information gap useful?
cards.answer: A concrete foothold, a meaningful missing fact, a stake and enough clues for the audience to form predictions.

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: Does empathy equal approval?
cards.answer: No. Dramatic alignment can make a character’s fear or logic intelligible without endorsing the character’s choices.

cards.name: Why can a story hurt, and still feel worth watching?
cards.q: Write it: do the final audience pass on your five pages. On each page write one sentence for what the audience knows, one for what it wants to know, and one prediction it might make. Add or cut one beat so the page changes that prediction.
cards.answer: Model: Page 4 reveals that the “ghost” has been switching on the porch light to guide Mira home. The audience reinterprets three earlier flickers, then predicts she will leave. The final page makes her stay and switch it off, turning a scare into a choice.

cards.answer: Polish and protect the script, then make a producible short or workshop it with actors. Build a clean portfolio with a screener, subtitles, statement, stills and rights records. Apply only where the current rules fit. In parallel, develop a feature sample for feature labs or Nicholl. Treat festivals and labs as selective opportunities, never as promises.

cards.name: How do you finish, and what is the road from Ahmedabad?
cards.q: Can you deliver the rewritten five-page short and a dated 90-day plan from Ahmedabad without making a career promise?
cards.answer: Model answer: THE PORCH LIGHT, polished five-page short FADE IN: 1. INT. MIRA’S ROOM, AHMEDABAD HOUSE - NIGHT MIRA, 23, records the empty room on her phone. The ceiling fan ticks. On the audio, a porch light clicks on outside. Mira checks the switch. It is already off. She starts a message to her brother: “I heard it again.” Deletes it. Records instead. The light clicks on. 2. INT. HALLWAY - CONTINUOUS Mira carries the phone and a screwdriver. The front door is chained. The porch beyond the glass is empty. A small red REC light blinks on the phone. A second click. Mira opens the electrical box. One loose wire trembles, though there is no wind. Her brother’s old voice memo plays by accident: “If it comes on, don’t follow it.” Mira stops the recording. The porch light goes out. 3. EXT. PORCH - NIGHT Mira steps outside anyway. The lane is dark except for a phone-sized rectangle of light at the gate. Her phone displays a new recording, made one minute from now: Mira breathing, then saying, “I’m sorry.” She looks back. The house is dark. Her mother’s bedroom window is open. Mira walks to the gate, not the light. 4. EXT. GATE - CONTINUOUS The red light is not a ghost. It is her brother’s old recorder, taped beneath the gate latch. Mira presses PLAY. His voice, weak and close: “I left because you kept waiting for me to come back.” The porch light clicks on. In its spill, Mira sees a suitcase beyond the wall, packed for her mother. She touches the gate latch. The recording continues: “Do not make her wait too.” 5. INT. MOTHER’S ROOM - LATER Mira places the suitcase beside the bed. Her mother wakes. MOTHER You heard him? Mira looks at the phone. The light outside clicks off. MIRA No. I heard you. She takes her mother’s hand. The phone keeps recording, but Mira does not press stop. FADE OUT. Why this is a rewrite: the repeated light is set up on page 1, the warning returns on page 2, the future recording turns curiosity into a choice on page 3, and the brother’s message reinterprets the object on page 4. Page 5 pays off the title through an actable decision rather than a twist. It is producible with two actors, one house, one porch, a phone and controlled sound. The dialogue is short because the images carry the history. 90 days from Ahmedabad, 1 November 2026 to 29 January 2027 1 to 15 November: save Draft 4, read it aloud twice, ask two trusted readers for notes on clarity and producibility, then make a dialogue and action pass. Fallback: record a table read if actors cannot meet.16 to 30 November: lock a two-actor, one-location plan, secure permission, budget sound and subtitles, and shoot a private proof of concept or the finished short. Fallback: make a clean recorded table read and revise the script from performance.1 to 15 December: edit picture and sound, create English subtitles, export a private screener, and keep the script, call sheet, releases and version history in a rights folder.16 to 31 December: screen it privately for five viewers, log repeated notes, and write a one-page director statement, 40-word logline, synopsis and stills list. Do not submit before the cut and subtitles are ready.1 to 15 January: shortlist three current, high-fit short-film festivals. Check their official rules, fees, premiere status, runtime limit, travel burden and what selection actually provides. Submit only if the fit survives the check.16 to 29 January: outline a feature or longer short that tests the strongest idea, read one legal screenplay, and choose one feature route to research for its next cycle. Measure success by finished work and a sound next decision, not acceptance.
